title: The baptism rite
hook: water, oil, a white garment, a lit candle, and a name

segments.voice: Yesterday, rite: worship done with the body as well as said. Your line was bodies remember.

Five things on a small table near the font: a pitcher of water, a little vessel of oil, a folded white cloth, a tall candle already burning, and a card with a name on it. A family holds a baby who has no idea what's coming. Or it's a grown woman in a white robe at the edge of a pool, shaking a little. In the Catholic and Orthodox rites, and in some others, all five things show up. In other churches it's water and a name, and nothing more. Either way, it's the rite that starts a Christian life.
screen: `A BABY, OR A GROWN WOMAN AT A POOL.`

segments.voice: Back in year one, this path looked at when churches baptize, infants or believers, and why. Today is about what the rite does with its hands. First, the water, at the center of every version described here. Paul says the person going under joins Jesus in his death and comes up with him: "buried with him by baptism into death," so that "we also should walk in newness of life." Some churches plunge the whole body, some pour, some sprinkle. The picture underneath is the same. Second, the name. Often a minister asks the parents, or the person, what name they give, and says it aloud over the water. Isaiah has God say to Israel, "I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine." A name spoken in front of everyone, tied to a promise. Third, the white garment. Paul writes, "as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ." Put on, like clothes. So in some churches the newly baptized are dressed in white, or a white cloth is laid on the baby. The clothes say what the water did. Fourth, the candle. Often it's lit from a larger candle that stands for the risen Christ, and handed to the family. Jesus told his followers, "Ye are the light of the world." Paul writes, "ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord." So the rite ends with a flame in a parent's hand, and a job: keep it going.

Light a candle, or a lamp, or just hold a hand open, for your baptism if you were baptized, or your birth if you weren't. Say your own name quietly, and think of who was there at the start: the people who held you, named you, hoped for you before you could hope anything. If you pray, thank God for them by name; if not, hold them in mind while the light burns.
The baptism rite. Water, a name, a white garment, a candle: the things a church uses to mark the start of a Christian life.
Your line: clothed in light. Put on like a coat, and kept burning. Go gently.

howItsDone: Christians baptize with water in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit; Catholic, Orthodox and some other churches add anointing with oil, a white garment and a lit candle, while other churches keep the rite to water and words.

chat.says: Why do they use a white cloth and a candle at a baptism?
options: They act out what the water means: putting on Christ like clothes, and now being light.
They're decorations added for the photos; the Bible never connects them to baptism.
They're the priest's own tools, so only clergy may ever touch the cloth or candle.
chat.meaning: Paul says the baptized have put on Christ and now are light in the Lord. The white garment and the candle show what the water did.

notes: Editor: the minister's question is now paraphrased without quotation marks, since it is not a public-domain wording.

Rite details: the Catholic Rite of Baptism includes anointing with chrism, a white garment and a candle lit from the Paschal candle; the Orthodox rite includes anointing, a white garment and candles. Stated as 'in the Catholic and Orthodox rites, and in some others'; confirm, and confirm the Orthodox details.
'What name do you give?' is paraphrased from the Catholic rite's opening question to parents ('What name do you give your child?'); presented as 'often' asked. Confirm.
Water is described as 'at the center of every version described here'; some groups (e.g., Quakers, Salvation Army) do not practice water baptism, which this day does not address.
Year one (day 152) covered infant vs believer baptism; today avoids repeating that angle.
Original: ἐνεδύσασθε is the verb form in Galatians 3:27; confirm spelling, accent and pronunciation.
